reason: The sources provide 13 verified claims about 2018 AH, including its size, discovery delay, and comparison to the Tunguska event.
story: In January 2018, a skyscraper-sized asteroid named 2018 AH zipped between Earth and the Moon—and we had no idea until it was over. The rock, estimated at up to 190 meters wide, reached its closest point on January 2nd, passing just 297,000 kilometers away. Because it approached from the direction of the Sun, its glare rendered the asteroid invisible to ground-based telescopes. Astronomers at the ATLAS survey in Hawaii finally spotted the object on January 4th, two days after it had already passed. If 2018 AH had struck Earth, the impact would have been catastrophic. Scientists compare it to the 1908 Tunguska event, which unleashed a 12-megaton explosion that flattened 80 million trees in Siberia. It remains one of the largest asteroids to ever come this close without being detected until after the fact.
angle: A 190-meter asteroid passed closer to Earth than the Moon, but astronomers didn't even know it existed until two days after its closest approach.

claims.claim: The asteroid reached its closest approach to Earth on January 2, 2018.
Astronomers did not discover the asteroid until January 4, 2018.
The asteroid was detected two days after it passed Earth.
At its closest, the asteroid was approximately 297,000 kilometers from Earth.
The asteroid passed closer to Earth than the Moon.
The asteroid's diameter is estimated to be as large as 190 meters.
The asteroid is categorized as an Apollo-class near-Earth object.
It was difficult to detect because it approached from the direction of the Sun.
The asteroid is similar in size to the one that caused the 1908 Tunguska event.
An impact would have released an estimated 12 megatons of energy.
It was the largest known asteroid to pass this close to Earth since at least 2011.
The discovery was made by the ATLAS survey on Mauna Loa.

disputed: Diameter estimates vary between 84-190 meters in most sources, but source S4 describes it as school bus size, which the script should ignore as an outlier.
The historical comparison for the last time a larger asteroid passed this close is listed as 1971 in S1 but 2011 in S5; the script should use 'largest in decades' to avoid contradiction.
